Adult Cape white seabream (Diplodus capensis) attain a maximum total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger members of the genus in southern African coastal waters. This ultimate length reflects the species' extended growing period, as individuals invest heavily in somatic development before the onset of reproductive activity. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 181.5 grams [Wwp = 181.5 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for local populations. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass of fully grown adults, has been estimated at 1871 grams [Wwi = 1871 grams], a value that underscores the substantial size dimorphism between juveniles and mature individuals in this iteroparous sparid. These morphometric benchmarks are critical for understanding the species' demographic structure and for setting size-based fishery regulations across its distributional range.

The lifespan of Diplodus capensis has been documented through otolith-based ageing studies of wild-caught individuals. Under the thermal conditions prevailing in its natural habitat, where water temperatures typically average 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], the species exhibits a maximum longevity of approximately 21 years [am = approximately 21 years], a relatively extended lifespan for a medium-sized sparid. The size at which 50 percent of individuals attain sexual maturity, a total length of 21.1 centimeters [Lp = 21.1 centimeters], represents approximately 47 percent of the ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a ratio consistent with the moderate-to-slow life-history strategy observed in many temperate and subtropical reef fishes.
